html:
Abdul Hamid II was sultan of the Ottoman Empire from 1876 to 1909, the last sultan to rule with real power.

He came to the throne in a crisis, and agreed to the constitution of 1876, which crowned the Tanzimat reforms. But after a disastrous war with Russia in 1877 and 1878 he shut down parliament and suspended the constitution, and ruled for thirty years as an autocrat, with censors and spies.

His reign saw heavy losses: Serbia, Montenegro and Romania became fully independent, Bulgaria largely so, France took Tunisia, and Britain took over Cyprus and then Egypt. The empire was bankrupt, and in 1881 he let foreign creditors run part of its revenue through the Ottoman Public Debt Administration.

He tried to hold what was left together:

  • He stressed his role as caliph, leader of all Muslims, to win loyalty at home and abroad.
  • He built schools, telegraphs and railways, above all the Hejaz Railway to Medina for pilgrims, and backed the German-built Baghdad Railway.
  • His forces crushed unrest harshly. In the Hamidian massacres of 1894 to 1896, tens of thousands of Armenians were killed.

In 1908 officers of the Young Turk movement forced him to restore the constitution, and after a failed counter-coup in 1909 they deposed him. He lived under guard and died in Istanbul in 1918.
